newsitem.title: CANADA: HORSE RACING-CIGAR GETTING READY TO LEAVE HOME.
newsitem.headline: HORSE RACING-CIGAR GETTING READY TO LEAVE HOME.

text.p: The empty stall syndrome is setting in for trainer Bill Mott as he contemplates life without a Cigar.
The great six-year-old thoroughbred likely will end his spectacular career Saturday in the 1-1/4-mile Breeders' Cup Classic race at Woodbine racetrack.

Mott, who has saddled the international super star for his unearthly winning streak of 17 of his last 19 races, describes the prospect of losing Cigar in human terms, as do so many when talking about racing's all-time leading money winner and the biggest heart throb to come down the backstretch in years.
"I think we all realise that it's time to shut it down and let him go on to a new career at stud," said Mott with more than a little premature nostalgia on Thursday.
Mott said he could not verify reports that Cigar's owner, aviation magnate Allen Paulson, is contemplating a $30 million offer to race Cigar, who already has won a record $9.9 million, in Japan.
But it was clear the 43-year-old trainer would like to see his horse go out in style in the premier race on horse racing's biggest day, before the inevitable ageing process sets in with a vengeance.

"We've all been blessed that Cigar has been a sound horse, knock on wood, for as long as he has. Generally if a horse is sound, there probably is no reason a lot of them can't improve and stay in good form through the four, five, six-year-old years," Mott said. "The one thing we can't do is change the ageing process."
Cigar, named by Paulson after an aviation check point in the Gulf of Mexico, will turn seven in April, 1997.

Mott explained his decision to bring Cigar from New York's Belmont to Woodbine on Wednesday rather than a week or so earlier, when many trainers bring their horses to a new track to get them acclimated.

"Any training that I put in during a seven-day period or 10-day period really isn't going to make him like it any more. He'll either like it or he won't," said Mott, referring to the relatively deep dirt track at Woodbine. "It worked in the past and that's what we chose to do this time. He is a horse that does adapt pretty well."

Cigar, the 4-5 favourite to win his second-consecutive Breeders' Cup Classic, will have to adapt again to going up against 6-1 second favourite Dare and Go, who last August in California at the Pacific Classic ended Cigar's victory streak at 16, leaving him tied with Citation for the modern record for consecutive wins.
Dare and Go's trainer, Richard Mandella, said he will "not allow myself to think that (Cigar) is vulnerable."
But Mandella thinks his horse is ready for the great Cigar, who turned out to be great only after failing as a turf runner.

"Dare and Go since he's been young has been able to go on the pace or take back," Mandella said. "In the (Pacific Classic) we knew what the pace would be and he cooperated. He wasn't cooperating that well in his last race (a third at Santa Anita on a disqualification on October 5) and he was a little too fresh. Hopefully, I have him smoothed out."
Whether Dare and Go is smooth or rough, Cigar will be attempting to run his best kind of race which "is to be in the stalking position and hope he'll do just what he's done in the past," Mott said.
"I feel he's as good as he was last year," Mott said.
